public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 800

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/800](https://www.erdosproblems.com/800)
- [Al94] Alon, N., Subdivided graphs have linear Ramsey numbers. J. Graph Theory (1994), 343-347.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos800

/--
If $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices which has no two adjacent vertices of degree $\geq 3$ then
$$R(G)\ll n,$$
where the implied constant is absolute.

A problem of Burr and Erdős. Solved in the affirmative by Alon [Al94].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_800 : answer(True) ↔
    ∃ C > (0 : ℝ), ∀ (n : ℕ) (V : Type) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
      Fintype.card V = n →
      (∀ u v, G.Adj u v → ¬(3 ≤ G.degree u ∧ 3 ≤ G.degree v)) →
      (SimpleGraph.diagonalGraphRamsey G : ℝ) ≤ C * n := by
  sorry

-- TODO: Add variants of the problem.

end Erdos800

review.notes:
The sole declaration, Erdos800.erdos_800, faithfully states Alon's Theorem 1.1. The paper defines a linear family using one positive constant independent of the graph, and Proposition 1.3 proves the stronger explicit bound R(G) ≤ 12n. Thus answer(True) and research solved are appropriate. The degree condition, quantifier order, cardinality hypothesis, real casts, and ordinary non-induced Ramsey-copy semantics match the source.

/workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles successfully. Independent proofs establish that the Ramsey-defining set is nonempty for every finite graph, that the empty graph has Ramsey number 0, and that an edgeless graph has Ramsey number equal to its vertex count. Consequently neither the natural-infimum default nor n = 0 causes a defect. Computations also confirm the degree condition accepts K₃ and K₁,₆ but rejects K₄.

Access limitation: https://www.erdosproblems.com/800 returned a Cloudflare challenge despite descriptive User-Agent headers and alternate access attempts. The mathematical statement and affirmative solved status were verified directly against the other cited source, Alon's complete paper; no declaration remains mathematically unverified.
